extracted.intended_audience: general readers and esports stakeholders (players, teams, organizers, developers, regulators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines, norms, and procedural standards for organising, designing, running, and regulating esports competitions and ecosystems, covering game design, tournament formats, player welfare, governance, and economic/legal issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design for professional play
rubrics_metrics.description: Many successful esports games have been designed to be played professionally from the beginning; developers may decide to add dedicated esports features, or even make design compromises to support high level competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: StarCraft II, League of Legends, Dota 2. Implication: game mechanics, balance, and features should support spectatorability, competitive balance, and high-skill expression. Anti-pattern: designing solely for casual single-player experience without regard to competitive integrity or spectating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectator features and broadcast delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Developers have added dedicated observing features for spectators, ranging from simple player POV to highly modified interfaces giving spectators extra information; the state viewed may be delayed to prevent teams gaining competitive advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design spectator UI to show informative views while protecting competitive integrity (use broadcast delay when needed). Examples: Counter-Strike series, Call of Duty, StarCraft II, Dota 2. Also includes newer VR spectating support (e.g., Dota 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Online play: latency and anti-cheat considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Online connections enable global real-time play but increase difficulty detecting cheating and introduce network latency which can negatively impact player performance, especially at high competition levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When running online competitions, mitigate latency (region servers, robust netcode), employ anti-cheat systems, and consider when to require LAN or trusted servers. Smaller tournaments commonly occur online; high-stakes events often prefer LAN due to fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local area network (LAN) for fair play
rubrics_metrics.description: Competitions are often conducted over a local area network which has very little lag and higher quality; physical presence helps ensure fair play by allowing direct scrutiny of competitors and preventing cheating such as hardware/software modding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use LAN for major tournaments to reduce latency and cheating. Anti-pattern: high-stakes events relying only on uncontrolled online matches without robust anti-cheat and monitoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developer-provided tournament support and restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Some developers require authorization for events featuring their games (e.g., Blizzard requires authorization for tournaments with more than US$10,000 in prizes) and may provide in-game rewards to authorized tournaments (e.g., Riot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tournament organizers must obtain developer authorization/licensing when thresholds or rules require it; failure may result in denial of support or legal issues. Developers can influence which events survive/are legitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team organisation, sponsorships, and roster volatility
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional gamers are often associated with esports teams or organisations that may sponsor players, cover travel/hardware, provide salaries, and represent players across multiple games; team rosters are often volatile and can change within a season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teams should formalise contracts, sponsorship disclosures, and roster management practices. Organisers and leagues should consider roster stability rules and transfer/trade regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Franchised league requirements (salaries and benefits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Franchised leagues generally require signed players to have a minimum salary with appropriate benefits and may share in team winnings; these leagues typically remove promotion/relegation in favour of franchise stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leagues using franchising should implement minimum salary and benefits standards, contract protections, and mechanisms for player movement (trades, free agency, minor-league pipelines). Example: Overwatch League, NBA 2K League.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion and relegation formats
rubrics_metrics.description: In many team-based esports organized play uses promotion and relegation to move sponsored teams between leagues based on seasonal performance; poor performers may be relegated while top teams from lower leagues are promoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use promotion/relegation to maintain competitive meritocracy; hybrid models exist (e.g., franchising with limited relegation for non-franchised teams). Consider stability vs. competitive mobility trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tournament formats and anti-cheating officiation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tournaments can use single or double elimination, group stages, or hybrids; esports tournaments are almost always physical events occurring before live audiences with referees or officials to monitor for cheating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose format appropriate to scale and fairness. Ensure referees/officials and anti-cheat measures (LAN, monitoring, rules) are in place especially for in-person finals. Hybrid/online qualifiers may require stricter integrity checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prize pool economics and sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Prize pools vary widely (major events can award millions); hosting large esports events is generally not profitable as a standalone venture and revenue sources differ from traditional sports (prize money, sponsorships, advertising, developer support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisers should plan diversified revenue (sponsorship, media rights, developer partnerships). Teams/players should not rely solely on prize winnings for long-term financial stability; leagues may guarantee salaries to provide stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Player training regimens and career lifespan
rubrics_metrics.description: Esports athletes often have extensive training routines (examples: Team Liquid practicing minimum 50 hours/week); players typically reach competition in mid-late teens and often retire by late 20s, with many careers lasting less than two years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clubs should implement sustainable practice schedules, rest/recovery, health monitoring, and career planning. Anti-pattern: extreme hours leading to burnout and short careers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Player health and welfare (physical and mental)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns include sedentary behaviour, eye fatigue, lower back pain from poor posture, repetitive strain injuries, and mental health issues (stress, burnout, depression); some teams partner with fitness brands or hire psychologists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement physical training, ergonomics, medical support, mental health services, limits on practice hours, and injury prevention programs. Provide access to sports medicine and structured off-game conditioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Player conduct and sportsmanship standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Players are expected to behave ethically, abide by tournament/association rules, and follow general expectations of good sportsmanship (e.g., sending 'gg' when defeated); breaches (verbal abuse, toxicity, collusion) have led to bans/fines/suspensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leagues and teams should define codes of conduct, disciplinary procedures, and education on sportsmanship. Examples of enforcement: one-year ban for verbal abuse, fines/denial of prize money for collusion, suspensions for match-fixing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match-fixing and collusion prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Match-fixing and collusion for profit are serious violations that have resulted in fines, bans, and denial of prize money in high-profile cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robust integrity frameworks, betting monitoring, and cooperation with legal authorities are needed. Example anti-pattern: unregulated gambling markets enabling match-fixing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-doping policies and drug sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports exist of stimulant and other drug use among players; some bodies have banned stimulants (e.g., league-level sanctions), while international federations' positions vary (IeSF signatory of WADA but had not outlawed PEDs in its sanctioned competitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leagues should adopt clear anti-doping policies, testing regimes, and sanctions (e.g., expulsion) consistent with athlete health and competitive fairness. Provide education on health risks of unregulated drug use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Player employment protections and contract standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns over organizations refusing to pay salaries and excessive training demands have led to rules like minimum salaries, required contracts, and allowances for players to stream for additional revenue (as Riot implemented).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leagues/organisers should require written contracts, minimum compensation, protections against exploitative practices, and transparency around working conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gambling regulation and youth protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Gambling on esports has varied legality by jurisdiction, has created black markets using virtual currency/items, raised underage gambling concerns, and led to regulatory scrutiny; some jurisdictions legalised esports betting with age/competition restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators and organisers should restrict underage access, monitor gambling sponsorships, and address virtual-item betting and skins markets. Anti-pattern: unregulated third-party gambling integrated with esports ecosystem enabling underage participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of data analytics and machine learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Machine learning and big-data analytics are used to analyze massive match datasets to visualize statistics, predict win probability, and advise teams on adjustments; some teams partner with software companies for predictive tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage publicly available match data for performance analysis, scouting, and strategy. Ensure data quality, ethical use, and secure handling of team-sensitive analytics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developer dependence and competition sustainability risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Because many esports competitions and leagues are run or supported by game publishers, a developer's decision to reduce resources or cancel tournament plans can make players' careers non-viable (example: Blizzard reducing support for Heroes of the Storm).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teams/players should diversify income streams; organisers should consider contractual protections and contingency plans. Leagues should assess long-term viability before heavy investment in a single publisher-driven ecosystem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcasting, casting, and media coverage norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Major esports events generally feature pre- and post-game analyst panels and in-match casting by play-by-play and color commentators; the internet is the main medium for coverage with mainstream sports outlets adopting esports coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in quality casting and analyst talent to improve spectator experience. Provide infrastructure for reliable streaming and consider formats that enhance viewer understanding (replays, stats overlays).

rubrics_metrics.name: Event hosting profitability and commercial partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional revenue streams (ticket sales, media rights, advertising, sponsorships) differ in esports; hosting large events often relies on broader commercial partnerships and is not always profitable as a standalone venture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisers should secure sponsorships, media deals, and developer support to subsidize events. Plan realistic financial models rather than assuming large prize pools equate to event profitability.
